deep.reconstruction:
The page is a scratch sheet. It continues the previous page's work on the logarithmic (two-dimensional) potential and mean values. It also holds a solid-angle formula, some self-corrections and pen trials.

(a) Figure and solid angle (top). The sketch shows a closed oval, an exterior point, a ray from that point to a boundary point, and a short normal drawn at that boundary point. Beside it Gauss writes dσ = ds·cosθ / r². Here r is the distance from the point to the element ds, θ is the angle between the normal and the ray, and dσ is the apparent size of ds seen from the point.
- If ds is a surface element, dσ is the element of solid angle.
- For a plane curve the correct angle element would be ds·cosθ / r (my remark). The 'rr' therefore points to the 3-D reading.
- This is the basis of the theorem that ∫cosθ dS / r² over a closed surface equals 4π, 2π or 0 according as the point lies inside, on or outside the surface.
He next writes ∫ ds·cosθ / r³. This is either a trial variant or the start of a field-strength integral. Its purpose cannot be decided from the page.

(b) Logarithmic potential. 'R.log(A − t) .. ∂ Im.log t' I read as Re log(A − t) · d(Im log t). With t = ρe^{iφ}, Re log(A − t) = log|A − t| and d Im log t = dφ. So the object is ∫ log|A − t| dφ, the logarithmic potential of a closed curve with the angle element seen from the origin. This is the 2-D analogue of (a).

(c) Line-integral attempts. 'p+qi, P+Qi' introduces two complex quantities, and '∫ p ∂Q' is a line integral built from their parts. '∫ dt·log r, ∂…' is annotated 'r functio arb. von t' (r an arbitrary function of t). Gauss then dismisses this line of attack himself: 'Dummes Zeug' (nonsense) and 'falsch' (wrong).

(d) Series. Gauss writes log A − t/A − tt/A² − t³/A³ …, marked 'L'. The intended expansion is log(A − t) = log A − Σ tⁿ/(n Aⁿ). The written terms omit the divisors 2 and 3, but the previous page has them correctly (−ρ²/2R², −ρ³/3R³).
Taking real parts with t = re^{iφ} gives log|A − re^{iφ}| = log A − (r/A)cosφ − (r²/2A²)cos2φ − … . He writes only 'log A − r cosφ', underlined. The term should be (r/A)cosφ; A = 1 may be intended.
Integrating over 0 ≤ φ ≤ 2π kills every cosine term. Hence the mean of log|A − t| over a circle |t| = r < A is log A, the mean-value property of the logarithmic potential.
The previous page does the weighted version with the Poisson kernel q = 1 + 2Σ aⁿ cos nφ. That gives (1/2π)∫ log|R − e^{iφ}| q dφ = log(R − a) = log R − a/R − a²/2R² − … for a < 1 < R. This is consistent with harmonicity of log|R − z| in the unit disc.

(e) 'troppo:' (too much) and a second 'L' are further marginal judgements.

(f) The bottom is pen trials and doodles, not mathematics: 'dear', 'dear', 'Dr D non est tam facile' ('is not so easy'), a name read as 'Spangenberg', repeated capital D's and 'seven'.

The next page moves on to Laplace's integral for Legendre polynomials and the expansion of 1/distance. The page as a whole is preparatory potential theory: solid angle, and mean values of logarithmic and Newtonian potentials.
errors: The series log A − t/A − tt/A² − t³/A³ omits the coefficients 1/2, 1/3: correct is log(A−t) = log A − t/A − t²/(2A²) − t³/(3A³) − … (the previous page has it right). The nearby 'falsch' / 'L' marks may or may not refer to this.
The term 'r cosφ' should be (r/A)cosφ unless A = 1 is understood.

dσ = ds cosθ/r² is the solid-angle element only if ds is a surface element; for a plane curve, as in the sketch, the angle element is ds cosθ/r. The following ∫ds cosθ/r³ is not justified on the page.
Gauss himself rejects the attempts with ∫p∂Q and ∫dt·log r ('Dummes Zeug', 'falsch').
Previous-page transcription: the kernel should be (1−a²)/(1−2a cosφ+a²), not 1/(1−a cosφ+aa).

results.what: Element of apparent (solid) angle dσ = dS cosθ / r² subtended by a surface element at a point
results.modern_name: Solid angle element; Gauss's solid-angle theorem (∮cosθ dS/r² = 4π/2π/0)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria attractionis 1813; Allgemeine Lehrsätze 1839/40), with antecedents in Lagrange/Legendre

results.what: Mean of log|A − t| over a circle |t| = r < |A| equals log|A|, via the real part of the log series
results.modern_name: Mean-value property of the logarithmic potential / harmonic functions in the plane
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (3-D mean value theorem, 1840); planar version folklore (Poisson, Gauss)

results.what: Weighted mean ∫ log|R − e^{iφ}| · Poisson kernel dφ = 2π log(R − a) (previous page, used here)
results.modern_name: Poisson integral formula for harmonic functions in the disc

results.what: Series log(A − t) = log A − Σ tⁿ/(nAⁿ)

deep.surprise_reason: These are fragmentary scratch notes on solid angle and the mean value of the logarithmic potential. This is material Gauss is well known to have developed in his potential-theory work (1813, 1839–40). Half the page is self-rejected attempts and pen trials.

checkable.asserts: Correct log series coefficients (1/2, 1/3), which the page omits; result should be 0
Mean of log|1 − r e^{iφ}| with r = 1/2 vanishes, i.e. the mean of log|A − t| on |t| = r < A is log A (here A = 1); should be ≈ 0
Poisson integral of log|R − e^{iφ}| with R = 3, a = 1/2 equals 2π log(R − a); should be ≈ 0
Poisson kernel series identity used for q on the previous page (|a| < 1); should simplify to 0
Laplace's integral for P_2 used on the next page; should be 0

transcription_corrections: 'R.log(A−t)..∂ Im.log t' means Re log(A − t) · d(Im log t), i.e. log|A − t| dφ.
'r functio arb. von t' = 'r functio arbitraria von t' (r an arbitrary function of t).
'log A − r cosφ' is underlined in the original; the coefficient 1/A is apparently omitted.
The bottom lines ('dear', 'Dr D non est tam facile', 'Spangenberg', 'seven') are pen trials, not mathematics.
